Nehemiah Coxe
nee-uh-MY-uh KOKS
proper noun (figure)
English personal name. Nehemiah (Hebrew, "Yahweh comforts"); Coxe (also Cox), an English surname. Nehemiah Coxe (d. 1689) was a Particular Baptist pastor, physician, and likely co-editor of the 1689 Confession.

📖 Biblical Definition

Nehemiah Coxe (died 1689) was a Particular Baptist pastor, trained physician, and the man most scholars credit as a principal editor of the 1689 Second London Baptist Confession of Faith — and the foremost early articulator of distinctively Baptist covenant theology. The son of Benjamin Coxe (himself a signer of the 1644 First London Confession), Nehemiah was a learned man who practiced medicine and pastored the Petty France congregation in London alongside William Collins. He is best known for his 1681 work A Discourse of the Covenants that God Made with Men before the Law, which set out the Particular Baptist understanding of the relationship between the old and new covenants — a covenant theology that affirms the Reformed framework of the covenant of works and the covenant of grace while distinguishing the Baptist position from the Presbyterian (paedobaptist) covenant scheme. The Baptist refinement holds that the covenant of grace is formally established and revealed only in the new covenant in Christ, with the Abrahamic and Mosaic administrations serving as types and shadows pointing forward, rather than as successive administrations of one substantially identical covenant of grace into which infants are born. This covenant theology is the doctrinal foundation of the Baptist position on the subjects of baptism: only believers, who are actual members of the new covenant, are proper recipients of the covenant sign. Coxe's likely editorial hand in the 1689 and his covenantal writing make him one of the most theologically significant of the Particular Baptist fathers, and the modern recovery of 1689 federalism (Baptist covenant theology) draws heavily on his work.

Particular Baptist pastor and physician (d. 1689); likely principal editor of the 1689 Confession; foremost early articulator of distinctively Baptist covenant theology in his 1681 Discourse of the Covenants; foundational to modern 1689 federalism.

NEHEMIAH COXE, proper noun. Particular Baptist pastor and physician (d. 1689).

Son of Benjamin Coxe (signer of the 1644 First London Confession); pastored the Petty France congregation with William Collins.

Credited by most scholars as a principal editor of the 1689 Second London Baptist Confession.

Author of A Discourse of the Covenants that God Made with Men before the Law (1681), the foremost early statement of Baptist covenant theology.

Foundational to modern "1689 federalism" — the distinctively Baptist understanding of the old and new covenants.

📖 Key Scripture

Jeremiah 31:31-32 — "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers."

Hebrews 8:6 — "But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises."

Galatians 3:16 — "Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ."

Hebrews 8:10-12 — "For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts... for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Nehemiah Coxe is corrupted when Baptist covenant theology is dismissed as a mere pretext for the baptism position rather than a serious federal scheme, when his editorial role in the 1689 is forgotten, or when modern Baptists adopt the 1689 while neglecting the covenant theology that undergirds it.

expand to see more

Pretext-not-theology misreading. Paedobaptists sometimes treat the Baptist position on the covenants as an ad hoc justification for refusing to baptize infants — theology reverse-engineered from a practice. Coxe's Discourse answers the charge: it is a serious, exegetically-grounded federal theology that works out the relationship of the covenants from the text of Scripture (Jeremiah 31, Hebrews 8, Galatians 3) before and apart from the baptism question. The Baptist position on the subjects of baptism follows FROM the covenant theology, not the reverse. To engage the Baptist position rightly is to engage its covenant theology, not to dismiss it as a pretext.

Confession-without-covenant-theology misreading. Many modern Baptists subscribe the 1689 while holding only a vague sense of its covenant theology — or while importing wholesale a Presbyterian covenant scheme that the 1689's own framers (Coxe foremost) deliberately refined. The 1689 has its own federal theology, distinct at key points from Westminster's, and that theology is the foundation of the Baptist understanding of baptism, the church, and the relationship of the testaments. The recovery of 1689 federalism — reading the confession's covenant theology on its own terms, drawing on Coxe — is the recovery of the confession's own doctrinal substance, not an optional academic refinement.
